succulent

SUK-yuh-lunt -- Latin sucus, 'juice, sap,' plus -ulentus, 'full of': full of juice. · adjective

Hear It

What It Means

Succulent is naturally juicy and tasty.

The market stall sold succulent figs that split open at a touch.

Example

A cook wraps a chicken in foil and leaves it in a low oven all afternoon; when it finally comes out, the meat is so succulent that it slides off the bone.

Meat that full of its own juices and flavor is exactly what succulent describes. Unlike 'delicious,' which is a verdict on any food at all, succulent points specifically to juiciness.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

tender: Tender means soft and easy to cut or chew -- a texture word. Succulent is about juice and taste together: succulent meat is full of its own tasty moisture. Overcooked chicken can still be tender while dry as paper; it takes juice to be succulent.

flavorful: Flavorful means rich in taste -- a flavorful broth, a flavorful spice rub. Succulent narrows it: the pleasure comes specifically from natural juiciness. A dry cracker can be flavorful; only juicy food is succulent.

mouthwatering: Mouthwatering describes food so appealing that you want it before the first bite -- it is about anticipation. Succulent describes the food itself once you bite in: naturally full of juice and flavor. A photograph of a dish can be mouthwatering; only the dish itself can be succulent.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

dry: containing no moisture

tough: hard and difficult to chew

Where it sits · how much delight the taste promises

juicy → succulent → luscious

juicy vs. succulent: Juicy is the plain everyday word that succulent dresses up -- both mean full of liquid, but succulent adds the promise that the juice tastes wonderful.

luscious vs. succulent: Luscious is richer and more sensory than succulent: succulent means juicy and tasty, while luscious suggests almost overwhelming sweetness or richness.

Build the Word

The pieces

root — suc-: juice, sap (Latin (sucus))

suffix — -ulent: full of (Latin (-ulentus))

Put it together: Latin succulentus joined sucus ('juice, sap') with -ulentus ('full of') -- succulent food is literally 'full of juice.' The juice-root barely survives elsewhere in English, but the -ulent ending shows up in opulent, 'full of wealth,' and turbulent, 'full of disturbance.'

Use the root in a new word: opulent: Her opulent jewelry collection filled three velvet-lined drawers.

Word Building

Word Choice

Succulent almost always describes food -- succulent meat, succulent fruit. It is also a noun in gardening: a succulent is a thick, water-storing plant like an aloe or a cactus, named for exactly the same reason, because it is full of juice.
